item.title: For Some in a Disrupted D.C., Grand Prix Is More Irritation Than Celebration
item.description:
Downtown traffic has snarled, as crews scurry to put up barriers, weld down manhole covers and even relocate traffic lights.

The National Gallery of Art has conducted vibration studies and put up protective panels around some of its outdoor sculptures, while other nearby Smithsonian museums prepared to reduce public access.

Airlines have rerouted flights, as the closest airport braces for a temporary shutdown. And at least one school within the exclusion zone has had to go fully remote.

Even before the first engine has revved in Washington’s first Grand Prix this weekend, the effects of turning a warren of museums and historic landmarks at the seat of government into a 1.7-mile IndyCar racecourse have rippled across the capital. And for some residents and commuters, the resulting disruptions are wearing thin in a summer that has been full of them.

“It’s putting additional stress on a stressful situation,” Jason Cummins, who commutes regularly from Baltimore to Washington, said on Friday as he walked near the race perimeter back to his parked car. His drive into the city, normally about an hour, had taken twice as long that morning, he said.

“I understand that this is the nation’s capital,” he said, “but there’s a lot of things that happen here.”

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the final major event in downtown Washington to mark the United States’ 250th anniversary, punctuating a summer that also featured a state fair exhibition, an Ultimate Fighting Championship match and a marathon Independence Day parade, concert and fireworks display. Many of those events also involved military flyovers, making them sonically inescapable for nearby residents.

And all of them have been heavily promoted by President Trump, in a city already wary of his attempts to leave his imprint on it.

For the race, Trump administration has planned a two-day extravaganza, complete with more flyovers, fireworks and an honorary presidential lap of the course. The main event will feature 25 drivers zipping around for 147 laps, crisscrossing the National Mall and making tight turns around some of the nation’s most iconic buildings.

Race organizers have handed out about 140,000 tickets to spectators, which is also being broadcast on Fox Sports. And Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, has recorded a number of promotional videos to hype the event, repeating what has become its patriotic catchphrase: “Freedom doesn’t ring — it revs.”

While the race is expected to draw crowds, it is also expected to hamper other activities in and around the city, such as the National Book Festival, which is taking place a few blocks north of the race perimeter on Saturday, and travel in and out of Ronald Reagan National Airport, which announced a three-hour shutdown to coincide with the prerace festivities on Sunday.

Yet organizers, federal officials and the city’s mayor, Muriel Bowser, have said they would be open to the race becoming a tradition.

“It’s not just fun and games for our city. These are events that draw tens of thousands of people to our city,” the mayor’s office said in a statement. “Those visitors stay in our hotels, go to our restaurants, they visit our neighborhoods. For D.C., that means more good-paying jobs and more opportunity for our workers and businesses.”

Representatives of the race organizers did not respond to a request for comment.

A day before the race festivities were set to begin, the streets around downtown Washington were eerily quiet, even for a summer Friday. Residents and commuters, it appeared, had heeded city leaders’ exhortations to use the Metro, or simply stay home.

But for those whom public transportation was not a viable option, the many street closures, which extended for blocks beyond the racecourse itself, had given the city a labyrinthine feel.

“I was down there, and I thought, I’m never going to get an Uber here,” said Richelle Smith, walking away from the race perimeter to find a ride home to Chevy Chase, a nearby Maryland suburb. “I’m trying to walk to where I can even catch one.”

“Why they doing a race downtown, I don’t even know,” one driver of a blue S.U.V. fumed audibly through rolled-down windows, as he pulled up to a stoplight on the edge of the race perimeter, and made a sharp right turn to detour.

Staging an IndyCar race in a city does not mean just throwing up barricades. City streets must also be turned into flat track. That means manhole covers must be shaved down, or built up with special epoxy until they are level with the street, and welded shut, so they do not turn into inadvertent projectiles as cars pass over them at speeds upward of 180 miles per hour.

More than 200 manhole covers were welded down along the course, Doug Boles, the IndyCar president, said during an interview on Newsmax this week, in which he also noted that several traffic lights had been removed.

A spokesman for the transportation department said that IndyCar was covering the cost of all such preparations, and that the Trump administration would work with city leaders to address any post-race impacts to the roads.

Washington also presents a denser urban environment than some other host cities for racecars to navigate. The course snakes around buildings, in places forcing drivers to make quick, successive turns at high speeds, and raising the risk of collisions.

“It’s going to be hard to pass here,” Mr. Boles said in the interview, noting that five of the course’s seven turns were at right angles. “Could be a little bit of carnage in this place.”

But while the promise of collisions may be part of the allure for some racing fans, they have only heightened the concerns of critics.

“For an event of this magnitude in such a symbolic, densely packed area in terms of historic sites and rare collections, an undertaking like this should not have been rushed,” Mary Okin, the assistant director of Living New Deal, a group dedicated to documenting and preserving public works projects from around the time of the Great Depression, said in an interview.

Last month, Ms. Okin sent a letter to the National Park Service, asking officials to take steps to protect the murals in Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building, which sits on Independence Avenue along the racecourse, from potential damage. She suggested that the federal government monitor the murals, install temporary sound barriers and conduct pre- and post-race damage assessments.

But the Park Service informed her that “vibration monitoring is beyond the role of the N.P.S. for this event,” directing her to address concerns to the people responsible for managing the individual structures.

Representatives for the Park Service, as well as several museums and government buildings along the route, did not respond to requests for comment.

Across the National Mall from the Cohen building, vibration studies were carried out at the National Gallery of Art, said Chris Abanavas, a spokesman for the museum, who added that it had put in place “measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities during the race.”

While Mr. Abanavas did not specify the measures, plywood structures were seen earlier this week around some of the outdoor sculptures and features, darkening I.M. Pei’s glass atrium skylight that erupts onto the museum’s grounds.

item.title: Nancy Kassebaum, First Woman to Chair a Major Senate Panel, Dies at 94
item.description:
Nancy Kassebaum, a three-term moderate Republican from Kansas who was the first woman to chair a major standing committee in the United States Senate, died on Friday in Manhattan, Kan. She was 94.

The death, at a hospice care facility, was confirmed by her son William Kassebaum.

As the leader of the Committee on Labor and Human Resources (now known as the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions) from 1995 to 1997, Senator Kassebaum won passage of legislation to insure the portability of health insurance coverage when workers changed jobs. She and the bill’s Democratic co-sponsor, Senator Edward M. Kennedy of Massachusetts, overcame months of opposition from Senator Bob Dole, the majority leader and her close friend, fellow Republican and fellow Kansan.

She had earlier played a role as Congress overrode President Ronald Reagan’s veto of a 1986 bill to enact economic sanctions against the apartheid regime in South Africa. As chairman of a subcommittee on African affairs, she met with the president, urging him to challenge the regime: “There is one person they might listen to, and that is President Reagan.” Instead, he warned of the threat of Marxist tyranny if apartheid fell. She joined 77 other senators as they overrode his veto.

Over her Senate career, which lasted from 1978 to 1997, her voting record was scored at 56 percent by the American Conservative Union and 37 percent by the liberal organization Americans for Democratic Action. On most economic issues, she voted conservatively. But from her first run, she supported abortion rights, saying in a campaign debate, “Abortions are seldom the right moral choice, but I feel there should be a choice.”

In a 2013 interview for this obituary, she said that because of her views on abortion and her support for a ban on assault weapons, “I couldn’t get elected today” in Kansas. She was a critic of President Trump’s since the 2016 campaign, and endorsed Kamala Harris against him in 2024. In recent years, she also endorsed Democratic candidates for governor and senator in Kansas.

She had no trouble winning her three terms, though, and was a heavy favorite to win again in 1996. But like many moderates, then and now, she had tired of the political strife in the capital.

In December 1995, after she announced her retirement, she told The New York Times: “The higher the decibel level gets, the more it’s like a boxing match. It’s really different from when I came here.”

A year later, in December 1996, shortly before her third and final term ended, she married former Senator Howard H. Baker Jr. of Tennessee, an influential Republican politician who had served as majority leader and whose first wife died of cancer in 1993. For years, they lived at his home in Huntsville, Tenn., and on her ranch in Burdick, Kan., which she said in 2013 was so peaceful that “at night the only thing I hear is the coyotes.” Mr. Baker died in 2014, at 88.

Burdick is on the edge of the Flint Hills, and she said that, of all her achievements in Congress, she was proudest of the establishment of the 10,894-acre Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in that region, as well as legislation limiting liability for manufacturers of general aviation aircraft, an important industry in Kansas.

Nancy Josephine Landon was born in Topeka, Kan., on July 29, 1932. Her father, Alfred Mossman Landon, an oil man known as Alf, was then running for the first of what would be two terms as a progressive Republican governor. Her mother, Theo (Cobb) Landon, was a pianist and harpist.

Nancy went to local public schools, graduated in from the University of Kansas in 1954 with a bachelor’s degree in political science, and earned a master’s degree in diplomatic history at the University of Michigan in 1956, the year she married John Philip Kassebaum, known as Phil, a law student there. They moved to Maize, Kan., outside Wichita, and had four children.

Politics had been the lifeblood of the Landon home as she grew up — all the more so after her father ran in 1936 as the Republican nominee against President Franklin D. Roosevelt. (Mr. Landon won only two states, Maine and Vermont, and eight electoral votes.) Often visited by leading Republicans, he remained a revered figure in Kansas until he died at 100 in 1987.

But before his daughter ran for the Senate in 1978, her political experience was limited. She had been elected to the local school board and served a year as a constituent services staff member for Senator James Pearson.

When Mr. Pearson unexpectedly announced his retirement, she entered a wide-open, crowded Republican primary with eight other candidates. She was separated from her husband at the time — they divorced in 1979 — and ran as Nancy Landon Kassebaum.

She never denied the value of name recognition. “It has been said I am riding on the coattails of my dad,” she conceded while campaigning, “but I can’t think of any better coattails to run on.”

She won the primary with just over 30 percent of the vote, then defeated the Democratic candidate, Bill Roy, with 54 percent in the general election. She was re-elected in 1984 and 1990, earning three-quarters of the vote both times.

In addition to her son William, she is survived by another son, John Jr.; seven grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren.

The only woman in the Senate when she was first elected, she bridled at the kind of commentary on her clothing and hair that would never be directed toward her male colleagues. She occasionally complained that those colleagues did not take her seriously. But she had experienced the same thing at home.

“My dad was adamantly opposed” to her 1978 candidacy, she said in 2013. “I think it was because he’d thought I’d lose, but also because he could not imagine a woman in the Senate. It was especially hard for him to visualize it was his daughter.”

In 1995, she said that one thing she would not miss after leaving was being asked, “What’s it like to be a woman in the Senate?” By then, eight women were senators — so, she said, “it’s no longer a big deal.”

Adam Clymer, a former Washington correspondent for The Times, died in 2018. Zachary Woolfe contributed reporting.

item.title: Judge Denies New Trial for Karmelo Anthony in Texas Teen’s Killing
item.description:
A Black teenager who was convicted of murder in the fatal stabbing of a white peer at a high school track meet last year will not receive a new trial, a Texas judge ruled on Saturday.

The teenager, Karmelo Anthony, 19, was sentenced in June after an eight-day trial centering on an altercation at a track meet in April 2025, in Frisco, Texas, a Dallas suburb, during which Mr. Anthony stabbed Austin Metcalf. Mr. Anthony and Mr. Metcalf were both 17 at the time.

Mr. Anthony was sentenced to 35 years in prison. The murder trial and sentencing inflamed racial tensions in Collin County, a predominantly white region of North Texas, and drew protesters outside the courthouse. Some called for justice for Mr. Metcalf, while others called for Mr. Anthony’s freedom.

After the sentencing, Mr. Anthony secured a new legal team to appeal his murder conviction and sentence. After hearing testimony on Thursday and Friday, a new judge in the case denied Mr. Anthony’s request for a new trial. Mr. Anthony’s lawyers had appealed the decision, which will now move to the Fifth Court of Appeals in Dallas.

Greg Willis, the Collin County district attorney, said in a statement that he had expected the court’s decision.

“The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process,” Mr. Willis said. “Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”

Lawyers for Mr. Anthony said in a statement that they would continue to explore legal remedies.

“This denial does not end our work,” Mr. Anthony’s legal team said. “We knew when we entered this case that this case might not be won in a single courtroom or with a single motion. We will keep advocating for Karmelo until the justice we seek is obtained.”

In June, Mr. Anthony secured a new team of lawyers, who were working pro bono. His new legal team claimed that limited access to the courtroom had violated Mr. Anthony’s right to a public trial, that the court had improperly instructed the jury and that prosecutors had prevented Mr. Anthony from testifying that he had acted in self-defense. (Mr. Anthony has not denied that he stabbed Mr. Metcalf.)

His lawyers also made a successful bid to recuse the original judge on the case, John Roach, from additional proceedings after he gave an interview to a local news outlet in which he expressed personal opinions about the jury’s verdict.

Judge Michael Chitty, who took over the case, heard from prosecutors and Mr. Anthony’s new legal team this week. Some of the testimony focused on an informal, so-called gentlemen’s agreement between prosecutors and Mr. Anthony’s original legal team in which they had decided to limit what they would share in court about Mr. Anthony’s and Mr. Metcalf’s character and past behavior.

Prosecutors had suggested an agreement in which “both sides try the case without character, reputation, or extraneous evidence” for either teenager, Mike Howard, who was one of Mr. Anthony’s lawyers, said in an affidavit.

But Mr. Anthony’s new lawyers argued that such an agreement had been too limiting during the trial, impeding Mr. Anthony’s defense.

For instance, prosecutors felt that the defense had violated the agreement by mentioning that Mr. Anthony had been involved in a chess club, according to the testimony of one of Mr. Anthony’s original lawyers, Toby Shook.

Mr. Howard said in the affidavit that prosecutors had said that “if we called Mr. Anthony to testify, character, reputation, and extraneous evidence pertaining to Mr. Anthony were in play.” Mr. Anthony then chose not to testify during the trial.

Testimony on Friday from Bill Wirskye, a prosecutor, shifted away from the agreement and focused on security concerns during the murder trial, such as death threats made against lawyers and others involved in the case.

Mr. Wirskye also said that some social media influencers and content creators had been “bad actors” in the case, spreading misinformation to attract views and clicks.

item.title: ‘It’s Been Terrible’: Thousands in Indiana Remain Without Power
item.description:
It was Day 11 without power in Gary, Ind., and Pierre Ervin was beyond fed up.

He could not eat breakfast in his dark, storm-damaged home because he had thrown out all the food rotting in his refrigerator. So he headed to work hungry on Saturday, threading his way past the snapped trees and downed power lines littering the industrial city as frustration grew with the agonizingly slow process of restoring power.

“It’s been terrible,” Mr. Ervin, 46, said.

About 30,000 customers across northern Indiana were still without electricity on Saturday evening, nearly two weeks after thunderstorms flooded neighborhoods and pummeled the region with hurricane-force winds.

About 56 percent of those people are in Gary, a majority-Black city of 67,000 that has long grappled with poverty, population loss and disinvestment as its steel industry shrank and homes and buildings were abandoned.

“My people are being overlooked,” said Myles Tolliver, a Gary councilman whose family has been staying outside Chicago while they wait for power to be restored. “Our families are sitting in the dark. We don’t need any more excuses. We need the lights on.”

On Saturday, as power returned to some customers across northern Indiana, Gary residents said they were angry and despondent to find themselves, once again, at the back of the line. The local utility, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co., said that Gary and the nearby city of Portage would be the last to have their electricity back, potentially by the end of Tuesday.

As they sat inside their dark living rooms or on porches to escape the stagnant air inside, some residents said they doubted a rich, white town would have been left to languish for so long without power.

“I don’t understand it,” said Daymond Willis, 45, a chef at a casino restaurant, who has been without power since Aug. 11. “It shouldn’t be this long. I think If we weren’t a Black city things would be different.”

On Saturday, some residents said a few businesses and apartments had gotten their power back, and more utility trucks were rolling through the streets. Steve Segura, a city spokesman, said the utility was sending an additional 85 line workers and 240 vegetation management crews.

But residents and politicians were increasingly exasperated.

Gov. Mike Braun of Indiana urged the utility to “match the urgency” of the people who had languished without power for nearly two weeks. Mr. Braun said on Friday that he requested an expedited major disaster declaration from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to bring in more resources.

“Bring in more crews,” Mr. Braun, a Republican, told the utility in a pointed social media post on Saturday. “Put every available resource into the field. Get creative. Get the job done.”

Northern Indiana Public Service Co. said its electric system had suffered “unprecedented and widespread damage” from the storm, and did not answer its 24-hour hotline for media inquiries on Saturday. An automated message said the voice mailbox was full.

On Aug. 11, Gary was pummeled by a derecho, a group of intense thunderstorms that last several hours, which brought heavy rain and damaging wind gusts of 99 miles per hour as part of a punishing parade of storms through Indiana since the start of spring. Through July, 89 tornadoes have touched down in the state this year, well above the annual average of 28, according to the National Weather Service.

“This has been a hyperactive season for us,” said Ricky Castro, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Romeoville, Ill., southwest of Chicago.

But there was some relief in the forecast, with a very small chance of thunderstorms in Gary on Saturday and drier weather expected in coming days.

Donations and supplies of food, tarps, bottled water and repair kits have flowed into Gary, and President Trump granted an emergency declaration last week. There has been no visible presence of federal-emergency-management officials on the ground, and FEMA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Meantime, residents have come together to try to help one another through the blackout.

Some have held sidewalk barbecues to feed their neighbors. Others with generators have opened their homes to let neighbors do laundry or charge their phones.

On Saturday, more than 200 people at the CityLife community center received a lunch of fried chicken, coleslaw, potato salad and biscuits that were donated by the singer Deniece Williams, a Gary native. About a mile away, a few hundred people lined outside a strip mall up for meals donated by two Chicago-based restaurants.

Ahmed Musleh, a manager of the Save More grocery store, said the market had given away 20 cases of water and grilled hot dogs for residents in need in its parking lot, about 500 feet away from where another community group had set up to feed residents.

Mr. Musleh said his store would be able to make an insurance claim for the food it was forced to discard, but he worried that his customers on food stamps would not receive the same help.

“They were already struggling, and for them to lose an entire month of food is a big thing,” he said.

Residents said the storm had already cost their families thousands of dollars in spoiled food, lost wages, hotel bills, fuel for generators and other costs of enduring the blackout.

Keya Reed, a 51-year-old warehouse worker, and her husband, Derrick Reed, a 57-year-old maintenance worker, said they had already spent $7,000 on a generator, gasoline and a tree-cutting service to haul away a tree that had downed power lines and damaged their modest home. Even as their costs pile up, they have refused to go to food pantries or take donated foods because, they said, others in Gary need it more.

Ms. Reed, who has lived in Gary her whole life, said she and others were used to dealing with the hardship.

“Everything is always against Gary,” she said on Saturday inside her home, its air dark and stuffy, the hallways tangled with electrical lines snaking to the generator. “It’s really sad to say, but I’m used to it.”

item.title: Violent Extremist Who Targeted Young People Online Is Sentenced to 77 Years
item.description:
A federal judge in Tennessee on Wednesday sentenced a follower of violent online extremist groups to 77 years in prison after he coerced 30 young people to send him nude images, abuse animals or engage in self-mutilation, prosecutors said.

The man, Kyle William Spitze, 27, operated under the groups known as Harm Nation and 764, prosecutors said. The three digits originate from the ZIP code of the group’s founder living in Texas, according to the Anti-Defamation League.

The groups are online networks that the U.S. Department of Justice has described as part of nihilistic violent extremism, a movement sowing chaos to usher society’s downfall.

They achieve their aims, in part, by glorifying mass murder and urging victims to engage in self-harm, the authorities said.

Mr. Spitze received the “longest federal sentence ever imposed on a nihilistic violent extremist,” John A. Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security for the Justice Department, said in a statement.

The sentence “sends a strong message that civil society will not tolerate such depravity,” he added.

Jonathan Cooper, a lawyer for Mr. Spitze, said in an email on Saturday that his client was a member of these groups because it was the only place where he could find validation and support he could not get from his parents.

Mr. Spitze, of Friendsville, Tenn., was not a part of these organizations because of their ideologies or dark principles, Mr. Cooper said.

He objected to “every single” accusation filed by the government, according to court papers filed by Mr. Cooper.

“The government portrayed Kyle as a demon, and many will call him a monster,” Mr. Cooper said. “However, it is the unfortunate truth that this young man is a product of his environment and our society.”

Mr. Spitze was part of online networks that relied on threats, blackmail and manipulation to get victims to produce or livestream self-harm and graphic content, prosecutors said.

The authorities identified at least 30 victims from around the world. One was 12 years old, according to court records.

Two victims, whose ages were not made public, died by suicide, the authorities said. One victim fled her country and changed her name to heal and feel safe, prosecutors said.

“The defendant’s criminal acts are a new breed of violence, so powerful the only tools the defendant needed were his phone and the internet,” prosecutors said in court documents. “During interviews with the F.B.I., the defendant’s victims outlined how the defendant was able to permanently scar victims across the world, physically and mentally, without ever having to lay a hand on them in person.”

The case began in December 2023, when the F.B.I. looked into tips that Harm Nation members had child sexual abuse imagery.

Discord, an online messaging platform, provided investigators with a report flagging members partaking in “high-harm activities,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze was among those flagged.

Investigators found he had pictures of young girls who cut themselves. The girls had written “Crim” or “Criminal” on their bodies with their own blood, which was a moniker Mr. Spitze used, prosecutors said.

Investigators searched Mr. Spitze’s cellphone after obtaining a search warrant in February 2024. They found similar images and videos, prosecutors said.

“The forensic examination of the defendant’s phone revealed the defendant had no legitimate employment, and spent countless hours finding, grooming and threatening victims,” prosecutors said.

One victim, a 12-year-old girl, began a casual and friendly conversation online with Mr. Spitze, prosecutors said.

Within three days, Mr. Spitze asked the girl to take nude photos of herself and sent her a graphic video. The girl also sent Mr. Spitze graphic footage of herself, prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze threatened to release those images if the victim did not meet his demands. She was also forced to kill a chicken and spell “crim” with its intestines, prosecutors said.

“Like a spider spinning a web, the defendant waited patiently, grooming his victims until he had them trapped,” prosecutors said. “The defendant then flooded his victim’s world with nonstop texting, direct messaging, video calls and demands for graphic content.”

Mr. Spitze pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child sexual exploitation material, one count of abetting the distribution of animal-crushing videos and possessing and accessing child exploitation material with an intent to view it, prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze regretted his actions, Mr. Cooper said, and experienced mental health issues and abused substances from an early age. By pleading guilty, Mr. Spitze sought to avoid a prolonged trial and spare his victims further trauma, he added.

item.title: Officials Investigating Mail Carrier in Peacock Assault
item.description:
Officials said they are investigating a mail carrier after video surfaced of him appearing to strike a beloved peacock on Tuesday in a Pasadena, Calif., neighborhood.

Gina Davis, a member of the community, said her husband called her after finding the peacock, known as Sugar, in the street.

Ms. Davis said that she found Sugar with a swollen eye and that he could not move one of his wings.

She said she had checked footage from a security camera that had a view of the street, a corner of her house and a neighbor’s house.

In the video, posted by the television station ABC11, the peacock appears to be on the opposite side of a fence from the mail carrier. The carrier then appears to spray some kind of liquid in the direction of the bird.

Moments later, the carrier, who was not identified, appears to hurl something toward the peacock, the video shows. Another part of the video shows the peacock directly in front of the mail delivery truck, before the carrier strikes it with an object.

Sugar then topples over before collapsing.

According to Ms. Davis, the man in the video is the regular postal worker in the neighborhood. She said Sugar followed him “a lot” while he delivered mail.

“Postal employees in this area have experienced previous encounters with peacocks, and the Postal Service has been working with Pasadena Humane regarding concerns involving the birds,” the U.S. Postal Service said in a statement.

The Postal Service said it was reviewing what happened “and gathering the facts.”

“We expect our employees to conduct themselves professionally and appropriately while performing their duties,” it said.

Flocks of wild peacocks are common in the area, and Sugar is no stranger to the neighborhood.

Ms. Davis said she lived in the neighborhood for 25 years and Sugar was around for at least four of them. There were a number of peacocks around, but Sugar was the only white one.

“The peacocks are used to people,” she said. “They walk up to houses, lie in nests and bushes of the front yards.”

It’s not uncommon for neighbors to feed the peacocks, she said, adding that some keep fruit and seeds on hand as snacks for the birds. Sugar’s favorite treat is blackberries.

The treatment and condition of Sugar left Ms. Davis disheartened. On a typical day, Sugar wanders around the neighborhood, she said.

“He loves to scream and talk and is vocal, and he’s usually the loudest,” she said. “Like our neighborhood rooster,” she added.

In an interview on Saturday, Kevin McManus, a spokesman for Pasadena Humane, said that Sugar was being treated for his injuries and continues to heal.

Sugar was eating and “moving about normally, and the swelling around his injuries has gone down a bit,” he said.

“Our veterinarians and wildlife team will continue to monitor him, and the prognosis is positive that he will be able to released back to the wild,” Mr. McManus said.

Georgia Gee contributed research

item.title: Jackie O’s Private Beach Is Open to All. But It’s a Hike.
item.description:
Alex Wilcox Cheek’s alarm went off a few minutes before 10 a.m. on a recent Sunday to reserve a parking space at a trailhead on the farthest tip of Martha’s Vineyard. The pressure, he said, was not unlike buying coveted concerted tickets.

He would later spend a morning among the trees — oaks, beetlebungs, maples — gnarled with time and salt spray from the Atlantic Ocean. He wondered, Had anyone ever seen these trees up close, in person?

It was a fair question. After generations of private ownership, more than 330 acres in Aquinnah, once owned by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and her daughter, Caroline Kennedy, opened to the public last year as the Squibnocket Pond Reservation, with a new trail added in July.

The property includes windswept moors, burbling creeks and an exclusive swimming beach. It not only offers a prime example of how one of history’s most famous families, back in the cultural discourse with shows like “Love Story” and a run at Congress, has enjoyed the privacy of natural beauty. But it also cracks open a corner of Martha’s Vineyard, so untouched, that other multimillion-dollar properties — and the affordable housing crisis created in their wake — don’t even seem to exist.

“There’s a serenity and a calm up here; it’s just been inaccessible in a lot of ways,” said Wilcox Cheek, who grew up coming to the area as a child.

But its inaccessibility, then and now, has worked in its favor.

“We’re really fortunate to have access to this corner of the island.”

In 1978, Onassis purchased the property, known as Red Gate Farm, for $1.1 million. Kennedy and her husband, Edwin Schlossberg, sold the land in 2020 for $27 million to two of the largest land conservation groups on the island, the Martha’s Vineyard Land Bank and the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation. (The property was once listed at $65 million.)

The reserve includes two separate holdings. The north entrance is a woodland walk, and the south entrance has multiple trails, including some that lead to a half-mile-long beach, and, new this summer, a trail that skirts along Squibnocket Pond. There, visitors can peer into an old hunting cabin where the former first lady once hosted lunches.

Next year, the land groups hope to make kayaks available to take onto the pond.

But getting there isn’t for the faint of heart. Parking spaces to access the south entrance are limited to 10 spots a day in the summer and require an online reservation. Cellphone service is sparse. Ticks are ever present. And it’s about a 25-minute walk down to the ocean.

“Our goal from the very outset was to sight the trailhead far away so that you had to walk to get there,” said James Lengyel, the executive director of the Land Bank. “And when you got there you would be rewarded by the remoteness and your ability to enjoy nature pretty much by yourself.”

In the late 1970s, Onassis told her children that “she had fallen in love with the rolling hills, wild dunes and silent ponds of Aquinnah,” Kennedy wrote in a letter to The Vineyard Gazette in 2019. “My mother believed that a North Atlantic summer was one of the most magical gifts in life.”

Red Gate Farm, named for the original gate that stood at the front of the property, “provided her with the sanctuary she needed and the freedom to be close to nature, her family, her friends and her books,” her daughter wrote. “It was a perfect expression of her romantic and adventurous spirit.”

Onassis was largely welcomed in town, both for her efforts in preserving the land and for keeping within the Vineyard way: biking to the Gay Head Lighthouse, paddling on her kayak, checking her lobster pots, grabbing ice cream with her grandchildren and keeping a low profile.

The bulk of the property’s sale took place in December 2020 for 304 acres for $27 million. A year later, the Land Bank bought an additional 32-acre lot from the family for $10 million. (Caroline Kennedy declined an interview for this story.)

The Kennedy-Schlossberg family kept the traditional Cape Cod-style house, guesthouse and surrounding 95 acres in the transaction. But if you’re hoping to get a glimpse of the Kennedy compound or run into Jack Schlossberg on the beach, you will be out of luck. The was preserve purposefully sited to maintain the family’s privacy.

Still, this land is steeped in Kennedy memories: John F. Kennedy Jr. could be seen windsurfing down on Squibnocket Pond in the 1990s, before he died in a plane crash not far from the family’s home. Tatiana Schlossberg, Caroline Kennedy’s daughter who died in January, was married at the family’s home in 2017. Many islanders can recall taking walks along the Atlantic beach, only to be turned around by an armed guard when the family was in residence.

Living year-round in a community where the economy relies largely on summer visitors has always been a difficult dance, none more so than in the last decade as soaring housing prices have trickled down to every facet of island life. But long before the concept of vacationland or a summer White House ever emerged, this land was — and remains — inhabited by the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah).

The Wampanoag have lived on the island, known as Noepe, for thousands of years, with a tribal community anchored in Aquinnah. The new reserve includes many sites like Black Brook and Witch Pond, which are rooted in Wampanoag mythology.

Tribal leaders said they were not contacted by the Kennedy-Schlossberg family ahead of the sale, and would have tried to find a way to bring the ancestral land back into their ownership or stewardship.

“Whether we purchase it or not, we should be considered,” Kevin Devine, the chairman of the tribe, said in an interview.

Tribal members do have special access rights to the land for sustenance purposes, including hunting and foraging.

“There has to be a balance between acknowledging the fact that we do have a housing crisis and we also have a development crisis,” said Tobias Vanderhoop, the secretary of the tribal council.

“The lands are sensitive. There has to be an eye toward acknowledging the fragility.”

“Every inch cannot be developed.”

In 2006, the Kennedy-Schlossberg family made a $100,000 donation to the town’s affordable housing committee as part of a new subdivision plan. For the Land Bank and Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation, that donation satisfied consideration of any further affordable housing needs on the property.

“When you look at the coast from Boston down to Washington, there’s very little that is natural,” Lengyel said. “So when you have an opportunity to protect something natural within those poles, you don’t trifle it away. You’ve gotta pay attention.”

But Juli Vanderhoop, the chairman of Aquinnah Board of Selectmen and a tribal member, said the affordable housing crisis facing the island, one that has forced many local families to move off-island, was too critical to ignore. Vanderhoop said she would have liked to see some of the property include housing, and for the tribe to have stewarded the land, as a way to support people who call Aquinnah home.

“What’s the responsibility of the conservation society to give back to the communities that hold these special places?” she said. “Really, I mean, because we’re losing them.”

Vanderhoop, who also owns Orange Peel Bakery in town, knows the magic of this corner of the island well.

“What has brought so much popularity to Aquinnah is the peace that this land brings to not just the people who live here, but the people who come back to our beaches, to this community, year after year after year,” she said. “It’s a peace that you can’t find any place in the entire world.”

Converting 336 acres of exclusive real estate into a nature preserve may not meet all of the island’s growing needs.

But the alternative — developing some of most ecologically diverse and sensitive land on Martha’s Vineyard — would have been far worse, tribal members said.

There are more than 30 rare species on the property, including spotted turtles, orchids and shorebirds. Adam Moore, the president of the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation, admired one of the oak trees on a recent morning, and noted the different trunks sprouting from the stump.

“That’s one tree that was probably cut at one time,” he said. “That’s why it has one, two, three — no four — major trunks.”

Moore continued beyond the sea lavender and patches of poison ivy, crossing over raised boardwalks that zigzagged across windswept dunes. The ocean was at first a sliver on the horizon, and then unfurled without another person in sight.

Be careful of getting lost in the beauty on the boardwalks, he cautioned. “I’ve almost fallen off this because I start looking out,” he said.

A seal bobbed its head up to say hello, as terns skated across the water’s edge. The state of the beach is in the hands of the tides — sometimes it’s sandy, sometimes it’s rocky. But one thing is for sure, Moore said, “It’s a knockout beautiful beach.”

item.title: Two Phoenix Police Officers Fired and Arrested After Violent Traffic Stop
item.description:
Two Phoenix police officers, who were accused of beating a couple and shocking them with a stun gun during an unreported traffic stop this month, have been fired and arrested on charges including kidnapping, aggravated assault and aggravated robbery, the police chief said on Saturday.

The officers, Luis Vasquez Jr. and Antonio Felix, were on duty when they stopped the couple at about 11:30 p.m. on Aug. 5 in south Phoenix, Chief Matthew Giordano said at a news conference. Detectives have confirmed that the officers physically assaulted both the man and the woman, and the investigation showed that a Taser was used on them, he said.

Neither officer reported the stop or activated his body camera, and there is no video of the encounter, Chief Giordano said. The police have not determined why the officers stopped the couple or what motivated their actions, and there is no indication that they previously knew one another.

The episode was so unusual that the police in Tempe, Ariz., who learned of it after finding the couple’s abandoned car, initially suspected that the men might have been impersonating police officers.

“When I was first made aware of the situation, I had the same reaction,” Chief Giordano said. “There’s no way this could be Phoenix police officers. It’s so far outside the bounds of our policies.”

The Tempe police report describes a harrowing and violent encounter.

The man told the Tempe police that he and his girlfriend were parked in his mother’s Dodge Charger when they noticed a police S.U.V. nearby. After they drove off, the S.U.V. followed and pulled them over.

Two officers got out of the S.U.V., tried to open the Dodge’s doors and threatened to smash the driver’s-side window, the man told the Tempe police.

The couple repeatedly asked why they had been stopped, according to the police report. One officer reached into the car and unlocked the driver’s door as the other put the woman in an “arm bar” and threatened to break her arm if her boyfriend did not get out, and then shocked her in the thigh and back with a Taser, the report says.

After the woman was handcuffed and placed in the S.U.V., the man said the officers shocked him with a Taser, punched him repeatedly in the head and pulled his hair. One officer drew a gun and threatened to shoot him while counting down from three, prompting him to get out of the car, according to the report.

The man then jumped back into the car and sped away alone, leaving the woman with the officers, despite threats that he would be shot, according to the report. He said the car later overheated and he abandoned it in Tempe. The officers removed the woman’s handcuffs, told her, “We know where you live now,” and drove away, leaving her to walk home, according to the report.

The Tempe police found the Dodge the next day with a broken window and tires that smelled of burned rubber.

Chief Giordano thanked the Tempe police for finding the abandoned car and bringing the case to his department’s attention. He said the department had also begun a broader review to determine whether anyone else was involved and whether there were systemic problems.

There was no indication that other officers knew about the encounter, and no other officers had been placed on leave, Chief Giordano said. He also said that Mr. Vasquez and Mr. Felix had previous policy violations, though none were “of this nature.”

The former officers also face charges of felony assault involving a bound and otherwise physically restrained individual, threatening and intimidating, criminal damage, hindering prosecution and tampering with evidence.
